results.title: Spillover Effects Definition - Intro to Public Policy Key Term | Fiveable
results.content: ## 🫘intro to public policy review. # Spillover Effects. Spillover effects refer to the unintended consequences that occur when a policy or action affects individuals or groups outside the intended target population. These effects can be positive or negative and often highlight the interconnectedness of social, economic, and environmental systems. Understanding spillover effects is crucial when generating and evaluating policy alternatives, as they can influence the overall effectiveness and efficiency of a policy decision. 1. Spillover effects can occur in various domains, including public health, environmental policy, and economic initiatives, making them relevant across different sectors. 2. Positive spillover effects can enhance community well-being, such as when an education policy improves overall literacy rates, benefiting society at large. 3. Negative spillover effects might arise from policies that inadvertently harm neighboring communities or ecosystems, leading to increased pollution or resource depletion. 4. Evaluating spillover effects requires a comprehensive approach to data collection and analysis to fully understand both direct and indirect impacts of a policy. 5. Ignoring spillover effects in policy design can lead to unforeseen consequences, reducing the efficacy of intended interventions and potentially exacerbating existing problems. * **How do spillover effects influence the generation of policy alternatives?**. + Spillover effects significantly impact how policymakers generate alternatives because they highlight the broader consequences of proposed actions. By considering both positive and negative spillover effects, policymakers can create more holistic solutions that address not just immediate goals but also unintended repercussions. * **In what ways can positive spillover effects contribute to the evaluation of public policies?**. + Positive spillover effects contribute to policy evaluation by demonstrating the broader benefits that a successful initiative can have beyond its primary objectives. Evaluators must consider these secondary benefits to gain a full understanding of a policy's impact. * **Assess how neglecting spillover effects could affect long-term public policy outcomes and societal well-being.**. + Neglecting spillover effects in public policy can lead to detrimental long-term outcomes as policies may unintentionally create adverse consequences that harm society. **Policy Evaluation:** Policy evaluation is the systematic assessment of the design, implementation, and outcomes of a policy to determine its effectiveness and inform future decision-making. ## "Spillover Effects" also found in:.

results.title: Cost Effectiveness Analysis Methodology – Happier Lives Institute
results.content: The goal of our cost-effectiveness analyses is to find the most cost-effective interventions and organisations that improve people’s wellbeing. If there is large variation in the effects of intervention (high heterogeneity), then our interpretation of an average value might be problematic (e.g., the studies might be so different that an average value might not represent anything meaningful). Typically, this will adjust down our estimated effect by some amount (which varies depending on the method) to account for the effect of publication bias (we discuss this in more detail in Section 9). * **Our modelling involves complicated parts that are not directly inputted into a meta-analysis.** Sometimes we need to combine different elements together (e.g., effects during different periods of life, different pathways of effect) to form the general effect of an intervention. We use this basis to convert SD-years to WELLBYs. To convert from SD-years to WELLBYs we multiply the effect in SD-years by our estimate of the typical SD on a 0-10 wellbeing scale, in this case, **an average SD of 2 points** on the Cantril Ladder scale (based on the Gallup World Poll data: 2,453 observations from 163 countries from 2006-2024 with a total sample of respondents of ~2,453,000)17. Ideally, we estimate the spillover effects using data from studies that measure spillover effects from the intervention directly. Reporting only a point-estimate of the cost-effectiveness has limited value, as it hides the statistical uncertainty of the estimate. This is the case for the cost of the intervention, the initial effect, and changes in the effect over time. But some variables – such as the total effect over time, the spillovers, and the cost-effectiveness ratio – are calculated by combining other variables, and the outcomes of these calculations are point-estimates. This involves running thousands of simulations to estimate the outcome (e.g., cost-effectiveness) using different possible values for the inputs (e.g., effect and cost). Note that we would typically constrain the initial effect so that it is positive and the trajectory over time so that it is decay (i.e., negative) if we have good reason to believe this is the case (e.g., results are statistically significant and well evidenced).

results.title: A comprehensive study to estimate income and price elasticities of household electricity consumption using Auto-metrics - PMC
results.content: # A comprehensive study to estimate income and price elasticities of household electricity consumption using Auto-metrics. We use Error Correction Models (ECMs) for each country to examine the long-term equilibrium relationships among key variables such as energy consumption, household income, electricity prices, and weather patterns, taking into account any observed anomalies and significant structural changes. The demand's income and price elasticities reveal how sensitive consumers are to changes in income and electricity prices, affecting energy conservation efforts and policy effectiveness. We use the Auto-metrics search method on annual data covering electricity usage, income, price, and weather variables to define an unencumbered error correction model for household electricity consumption. Findings suggest that long-run income elasticities are consistently below one, and long-run price elasticities are also below one in total value across all countries, indicating electricity is treated as a conventional good and consumption is not highly sensitive to price changes. Error correction models are used for each country to identify a co-integrating link among explanatory variables such as energy use, income, and electricity price. Summarizes the research on modeling household electricity consumption utilizing aggregate data, including both long- and short-term elasticities. The long-term cost elasticities estimated for all countries vary less than one, indicating that residential electricity consumption is inflexible to price in the short and long term. Variations in predicted elasticities can be attributable to several factors, as highlighted by meta-analysis studies [55], including the specifications of the consumption model and the estimation method, the type of data (i.e., time series information vs. All 12 countries have somewhat cost-inelastic demand for household power, meaning that any strategy focused on energy efficiency utilizing just price increases would have little effect on decreasing electricity usage and would result in a substantial loss in the welfare of consumers. This paper aims to add to the existing research on evaluating price and revenue elasticities for household energy demand by utilizing an original econometric methodology based on the automatic choice of model, saturating methods, and Auto-metrics. * 36.Al-Mulali U., Fereidouni H.G., Lee J.Y.M.
